summary: This unit teaches you to facilitate continuous improvement in your team. You will learn to make improvement part of normal work, define problems with data, run improvement meetings with proven techniques, test and put in place changes, measure results, coach and recognise team members, and make improvements stick and share them.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It teaches you to **facilitate continuous improvement** in your team: to help the people who do the work find problems, understand their causes, choose and test better ways of working, make the change stick and share what they learn.

**Continuous improvement** means making many small, steady improvements to the way work is done, rather than waiting for a big change from above. The people closest to the work usually know where time, money and quality are lost. A team leader's job is not to solve every problem herself. It is to **facilitate**: to guide the team to find, test and apply improvements.
**Who it is for:** team leaders and supervisors in offices, shops, hotels, call centres, warehouses, schools and public bodies.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Make improvement part of normal work
Set up regular routines (huddles, a weekly slot, a visible board) and link the team's work to the organisation's goals.
Use data, process maps and cause tools to write a clear problem statement and a measurable target.
Plan an agenda, set ground rules, use techniques so that everyone contributes and handle difficult behaviour.
Rank ideas, run a trial, plan resources and agree changes with others affected.
Work out percentages, averages and savings, and show results on a run chart or board.
Use coaching questions (GROW), respond to resistance and recognise contributions fairly.
Make improvements stick and share them
Write standard work, train people, check that it is followed, and pass good ideas to other teams.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with scenarios and short calculations.
A **written paper** with exact terms and longer answers.
**Practical group tasks**: facilitating a 45-minute improvement meeting in role play, and building a team improvement board with standard work and a 30-day follow-up plan.

blocks.note: In a facilitation question, the best answer almost always keeps ideas coming from the team, uses data rather than opinion, protects safety and quality, and follows up.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: The facilitator's role and making improvement routine

head: Aspect
Command and control
Facilitator
rows: The whole team, with the leader's help
The team, within agreed limits, with the leader removing obstacles
Slow: people resist what is imposed
Faster: people support what they helped to create
Ask questions, guide the process, keep to the facts and the time

blocks.p: A **facilitator** guides a group through a meeting or problem-solving process without imposing her own solution. She stays neutral on the content, protects the process, makes sure all voices are heard and keeps the group on the topic and the clock. The leader can still make the final call where authority demands it, but she says so openly.

blocks.h: Linking improvement to the organisation's goals

blocks.p: Before a team chooses what to improve, the leader should explain **how the team's work links to the organisation's goals** (for example faster claims, fewer errors, happier guests, lower cost). People then choose problems that matter, and the manager is more likely to support the change.

head: Routine
What it is
Benefit
rows: A short stand-up meeting, often at the start of a shift (5 to 10 minutes)
Raise yesterday's problems, agree quick fixes, share the day's targets
30 to 60 minutes set aside to review measures and ideas
Improvement becomes planned work, not an extra
A whiteboard showing targets, results, problems and the status of each idea
Everyone sees progress and problems at a glance
A simple way to submit and track suggestions
A list of agreed tasks, owners and dates kept from meetings
Tracks who does what by when

blocks.note: People stop suggesting ideas when nothing happens to them. Reply to every suggestion, even when the answer is 'not now', and say why.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **KPIs** (key performance indicators) are the main measures a team uses to track its results, such as calls answered, errors per week or room turnaround time. Choose a few that show whether the team is improving and display them where the team can see them.
Start with the problem, not the solution. Teams that jump to solutions fix the wrong things.
'Customers are unhappy' is a feeling, not a problem statement. A good statement is **specific, measured and factual**, and does not blame or suggest the solution.

head: Weak
Better
rows: In May, claims took an average of 18 days to settle; the target is 10 days
Between 1 and 28 March, 36 of 1,200 enrolment forms (3%) had errors
We are always short of stock
Stock-outs on 14 lines in April, causing 31 lost sales

blocks.p: A target should be **S**pecific, **M**easurable, **A**chievable, **R**elevant and **T**ime-bound. 'Cut average call waiting to 2 minutes by March' is a good target. 'Improve call waiting' is not.

blocks.h: Finding the facts and the causes

head: Tool
What it does
Example
rows: Counts how often each kind of problem occurs
Tally of reasons for delay in prescriptions
Ranks causes from biggest to smallest so the team works on the few that cause most of the problem
Two causes account for 70% of delays
Shows every step of the work as it is done, to spot delays, repeats and hand-offs
Map of how a claim moves from desk to desk
Ask 'why?' repeatedly until you reach a cause the team can fix
Why late? No stock. Why? Reorder late. Why? No one checks the stock sheet
Groups possible causes (people, method, materials, equipment, environment, measurement)
A line of results over time

blocks.p: Test the team's belief about the cause with **data**, not opinion. If the team thinks late deliveries are caused by traffic, collect data on late deliveries (time, route, driver, cause) and check.

blocks.h: Waste: where time and money are lost

blocks.p: Lean thinking lists common forms of waste: defects (errors and rework), waiting, unnecessary movement, unnecessary transport, over-processing (extra steps), over-production, excess inventory and unused talent (ideas not used). Looking for waste gives a team a practical list of things to remove. A tidy, labelled workplace (often called **5S**: sort, set in order, shine, standardise, sustain) also removes waste.
Group guest or customer comments into **themes** and act on the top ones first. A few loud comments are not a pattern. Counting them shows which problems matter most.

blocks.note: Record a **baseline** before changing anything: the starting figure (for example 24 minutes average wait). Without a baseline you cannot show that anything improved.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Planning and running an improvement meeting

ul: Say what the meeting is for: one aim, written in a sentence.
Send a short **agenda** with the aim, times and any data to read.
Invite the people who do the work and anyone whose work will be affected.
Book a suitable room and the materials (flipchart, sticky notes, dots).
Agree roles: facilitator, timekeeper, note-taker.
State the aim and the time available.
Agree **ground rules**: one person speaks at a time; all ideas are heard; no ideas are laughed at; phones away; stay on the topic.
Show the problem statement and the data.

head: Stage
Technique
How it works
rows: Many ideas, no judging, build on others' ideas
Each person speaks in turn; anyone may pass
Silent writing of ideas, then list all, discuss, rank privately
Each member gets 3 dots to place on favourite ideas. Six members with 3 dots = 18 dots in total
Put each idea on a grid. High impact, low effort ideas are taken up first
Everyone can live with and support the decision, even if it was not their first choice

head: Situation
What the facilitator does
rows: Use round-robin or silent writing; thank the person and ask for others' views
Ask them by name for a view, use small groups or written ideas first
Remind the group that ideas are not judged yet
An important point is off the agenda
Note it on a **parking lot** sheet and come back to it later
Calm things, summarise both views and return to the data
'We tried that before and it failed'
Ask what happened then and what was learned; conditions may have changed
Everyone agrees very quickly and no one questions
This may be **groupthink**: ask 'what could go wrong?' and invite a devil's advocate
Some members do less because others will cover
This is **social loafing**: give each person a clear task and make contributions visible

ul: Summarise the decisions.
Record actions in the **action log**: what, who, by when.
Agree the next meeting date.
Ask for a quick check: what worked and what could be better?

blocks.note: Do not let a quiet meeting fool you. Silence is not agreement. Check with each person, in a round, before you write 'agreed'.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Choosing, testing and putting improvements in place

ul: Rank ideas using an impact-effort matrix, dots or a scoring table.
Check each idea against **safety, quality, legal and customer requirements**. An idea that saves time by removing a safety step is rejected, and the team looks for savings elsewhere.
Estimate cost, benefit and time to put in place.
Check who else is affected: if a change alters the form that the accounts department receives, agree the change with accounts **before** it is made.

flow: Plan: set the target, analyse the cause, choose the change
Do: try it in a small, safe trial (for example one shift or one aisle)
Check: compare the results with the baseline and the target
Act: adopt it, adjust it or drop it, then plan the next cycle

blocks.p: A short **trial** on one shift or in one area, with results tracked, lets the team learn at low risk before changing everything.

A **kaizen event** is a short, focused improvement project, often two to five days, in which a small team redesigns one process and puts the changes in place. Compare it with steady weekly improvement:

head: Aspect
Kaizen event
Steady weekly improvement
rows: A few days, team away from normal work
Needs scope, team, data and sponsor support
A process with obvious waste that needs quick, joint effort

blocks.p: Before a kaizen event, agree the **scope** (what is in and out), the **team**, the **data to collect** and the target. A **sponsor** is the senior manager who supports a larger project, provides resources and removes obstacles.

A team that spends staff time on improvement should count it. **Payback period** = cost ÷ saving per period. Example: a 3-day event with 4 staff working 8 hours a day uses 4 × 3 × 8 = 96 staff-hours. If the new method saves 6 hours a week, the time is paid back in 96 ÷ 6 = 16 weeks.
If a team needs a small sum of money to test an idea, the team leader should put a short case to her manager with the costs and the expected gains.

If members say that improvement meetings leave no time for their normal work, **plan time for it**, share the tasks fairly and keep meetings short. Improvement that is added on top of a full workload fails.

ul: Tell everyone affected what is changing, why and when.
Update written procedures and forms.
Brief other teams and managers who depend on your output.
Show the target and progress on the board.

blocks.p: Improvement is shown by **data**. Compare the same measure before and after the change, using the same method.

head: Measure
Formula
Example
rows: Resolved first time 70% to 85% of 400 calls = 15 points = 60 more calls
9 people in a 15-minute huddle, 5 days a week = 9 × 0.25 × 5 = 11.25 hours

blocks.p: A **run chart** plots a result over time (for example weekly complaints for six weeks before and six after a change). It shows the **pattern** and the normal ups and downs, which a comparison of two single days cannot do. Mark when the change was made. One good week is not proof.
An **A3 report** is a one-page summary of an improvement: the problem, the current state, the causes, the actions, the results and the next steps. It forces clear thinking and is easy to share.

blocks.note: Always state the **baseline**, the **target** and the **result** together. A figure on its own, such as '6 errors', means nothing without what it was before.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: When a team member brings a problem to you, the best reply is often a question: 'What do you think is causing it?' This builds her skill and confidence. The **GROW** model gives a structure.

head: Step
Meaning
Example question
rows: What does she want to achieve?
'What would you like the error rate to be by June?'
'How many receipts out of 50 had errors last week?'
What will she do, and by when?
'What will you do first, and when will you tell me how it went?'

ul: Recognise promptly and **specifically**: say what the person did and what difference it made.
Share the credit with everyone who helped.
Match the recognition to the achievement: a thank-you at a meeting and sharing the results suits a team that cut invoice errors by half.
Be fair: use the same standards for everyone, so recognition does not look like favouritism.
Do not overload the willing: a person whose idea worked should not automatically get all the extra work.
Without recognition, people may stop offering ideas.

blocks.p: Thank a staff member who **reports her own mistake**. If she is blamed, she and others will hide problems; if she is thanked, problems come out early and can be fixed.

head: What you hear
Possible reason
What to do
rows: Past failure, or fear of repeat
Ask what happened and what was learned
Plan time and share the load
Fear of being wrong or not being heard
Clarify roles and the benefit to the team

blocks.note: Ask your team how well you facilitate: what helped, what did not. Reflect, and change one thing at the next meeting.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Making improvements stick and sharing them

blocks.p: Many improvements fade after a few weeks. People drift back to the old way unless the new method becomes **standard work**.

flow: Write the improved method as simple, clear, numbered steps (with photos if useful)
Train everyone, including new starters, in the **current** method and explain why
Check regularly that the method is followed
Measure the result and show it on the board
Review after 30 days, then at intervals
If results slip, check first whether the new method is being followed

blocks.p: If two months after a change the error rate begins to creep back up, the first question is **whether the new method is still being followed**, not whether the idea was wrong.
A new member who joins after a change should be trained in the **current** method and told why it changed. Otherwise the old habits return through the newcomer.

ul: Share a good result with your manager so that it is noticed.
Pass it to other branches or teams who do the same job; one team's solution may save others a month's work.
Tell customers, where it affects them.
Keep an improvement log so ideas are not lost when people move.

blocks.p: When a team meets its target, the team leader should **celebrate, standardise and pick the next issue**. Continuous improvement never ends: the same method (find, define, cause, trial, standardise, measure) is used again.

ul: explain what a facilitator does and how she differs from a command-and-control leader
set up huddles, a weekly slot, a board and an action log, and link them to the organisation's goals
write a factual problem statement and a SMART target, with a baseline
use a check sheet, Pareto chart, 5 Whys, process map and run chart
plan an improvement meeting with an agenda, ground rules and roles
use brainstorming, round-robin, nominal group technique, affinity diagrams, multivoting and an impact-effort matrix
handle domination, silence, groupthink, social loafing and 'we tried that before'
run a trial using plan, do, check, act, and plan a kaizen event
work out percentages, errors per 1,000, means, staff-hours and payback
coach with the GROW model and recognise contributions fairly
write standard work, train people and check that a change holds
share improvements with other teams and managers

terms: Many small, steady improvements to how work is done.
A person who guides a group through a process without imposing her own solution.
A short stand-up team meeting to review the day and raise problems.
Key performance indicator: a main measure of results.
The starting figure before a change.
A chart ranking causes so the biggest are tackled first.
Asking 'why?' repeatedly to reach a root cause.
Generating many ideas without judging them.
Silent idea writing, listing, discussion and private ranking.
Using dots or votes to narrow a long list.
A grid sorting ideas by benefit and difficulty.
A decision everyone can live with and support.
Agreeing quickly to keep the peace without testing the idea.
Putting in less effort in a group because others will cover.
A sheet for off-topic points to deal with later.
Agreed tasks with owners and dates.
A short, focused project redesigning one process.
The senior manager who supports a project and removes obstacles.
A line of results over time.
A one-page summary of an improvement.
The agreed best method, written down and taught.

c1.title: Waiting times at a St Ann's Bay pharmacy
c1.text: The pharmacy team in St Ann's Bay is asked to cut the time customers wait for a filled prescription. In March the average wait was 24 minutes; the manager wants it down to 15 minutes by 30 June. Over four weeks the team tallied 200 delays: insurance checks 90, medicine out of stock 50, unclear handwritten prescriptions 30, staff breaks at the same time 20, other reasons 10.

c2.title: Enrolment form errors at a Spanish Town registry
c2.text: The registry of a vocational school in Spanish Town handled 1,200 enrolment forms in March, and 36 contained errors. Eight staff meet to choose an improvement. The senior clerk speaks first and most; two clerks say nothing. Staff offer 15 ideas, and the facilitator, Ms Hines, wants a fair way to narrow them.

c3.title: A kaizen event in a Santa Cruz warehouse
c3.text: A distribution warehouse in Santa Cruz plans a 3-day kaizen event in which 4 staff, working 8 hours a day, will redesign the picking area. The team expects the new layout to save 6 hours of staff time a week. The pickers walk 80 metres per order now, and a proposal on the table would cut it to 56 metres. A member suggests stacking pallets in front of the fire exit to shorten the walk.

c4.title: Coaching and recognition at a Morant Bay municipal office
c4.text: A municipal corporation's customer service counter in Morant Bay has six clerks. Shelly-Ann, a clerk, tells her supervisor, Mr Reid, that she makes too many mistakes on receipts and wants to improve. Last week 7 of her 50 receipts had errors. Another clerk, Winston, reports that he made an error that cost the office J$6,000 in a refund. A third clerk's idea for a new queue ticket was tested by the whole team, and queue times fell.

c5.title: Making a change stick at a Half-Way Tree courier counter
c5.text: A courier firm's counter team in Half-Way Tree has six staff and a leader. Weekly invoice errors for the four weeks before a new checklist were 16, 14, 18 and 12. In the four weeks after, they were 8, 6, 7 and 3. Two months later the weekly errors have risen to 11.

questions.q: Which is the best problem statement for the pharmacy team?
o: Customers complain that the pharmacy is always too slow
Pharmacists are not working fast enough to meet demand
March waits averaged 24 minutes; target is 15 by 30 June
We need a new computer system to speed up insurance checks
questions.why: A good statement is specific, measured and factual, gives the target and date, and does not blame people or assume a solution.

questions.q: Using the tally, which causes should the team work on first?
o: Insurance checks and stock-outs, which together are 70% of delays
Staff breaks and other reasons, which are the easiest
Unclear prescriptions, because doctors cause most errors
All five causes at once so that none is missed
questions.why: 90 + 50 = 140 of 200 delays = 70%. A Pareto approach tackles the few biggest causes first, where most of the gain lies.

questions.q: After changes, the average wait falls from 24 to 18 minutes. What is the percentage reduction?
questions.why: Reduction = (24 − 18) ÷ 24 × 100 = 25%. Dividing by the new figure (18) would wrongly give 33%.

questions.q: The team finds that insurance checks cause delays. Which tool helps them to reach the root cause?
o: A run chart
5 Whys
A kaizen event
A parking lot
questions.why: Asking 'why?' repeatedly leads from the symptom (long checks) to a cause the team can fix, for example missing details at the counter. A run chart shows change over time but not the cause.

questions.q: How many errors were there per 1,000 enrolment forms in March?
questions.why: 36 ÷ 1,200 × 1,000 = 30 per 1,000 (3%). 36 is the count of errors, not the rate per 1,000.

questions.q: The senior clerk dominates and two clerks are silent. Which step best gives everyone a voice?
o: The senior clerk chairs and summarises every point
Ms Hines asks for a show of hands on each idea
The meeting is held without the senior clerk
Everyone writes ideas silently before any discussion
questions.why: Silent writing first gives quiet members equal input and prevents early ideas from anchoring the group. Letting the dominant person lead, or excluding her, does not build participation.

questions.q: Each of the eight staff receives 3 dots to place on the ideas they like best. How many dots will be placed in total?
questions.why: 8 people × 3 dots = 24 dots. Multivoting narrows a long list quickly to the top choices.

questions.q: During the meeting, a clerk raises a complaint about parking, which is not on the agenda. What should Ms Hines do?
o: Spend ten minutes discussing it at once
Tell the clerk the complaint is unimportant
Note it on a parking lot sheet for later
Add it to the list of ideas to vote on
questions.why: A parking lot records important off-topic points so they are not lost but do not derail the meeting. Ignoring or dismissing the point harms trust.

questions.q: What is the payback period of the kaizen event if the team saves 6 hours a week?
o: 12 weeks
4 weeks
16 weeks
96 weeks
questions.why: The event uses 4 × 3 × 8 = 96 staff-hours. 96 ÷ 6 = 16 weeks. Check: 16 × 6 = 96.

questions.q: The proposed layout would cut the walk from 80 to 56 metres per order. What is the percentage reduction?
questions.why: (80 − 56) ÷ 80 × 100 = 30%. Dividing by 56 would wrongly give 43%.

questions.q: A member proposes stacking pallets in front of the fire exit to shorten the walk. What should the facilitator do?
o: Allow it during the event only
Put it to a vote, since it saves 24 metres
Ask the sponsor to approve the stacking
Reject it as unsafe and look for savings elsewhere
questions.why: Safety and legal requirements are not negotiable. An improvement that blocks an exit must be refused, and the team finds savings that do not reduce safety.

questions.q: The team tries the new layout in one aisle for two weeks and records the pick times. Which PDCA stage is this?
o: Plan, since the team is still preparing
Do, then check
Act, since the change is being adopted
The last stage, since it tests the whole change
questions.why: A small trial is the 'do' step, and recording and comparing results is the 'check' step. Only after checking does the team 'act' by adopting, adjusting or dropping the change.

questions.q: In the GROW model, which of Mr Reid's questions belongs to the Reality step?
o: 'What would you like the error rate to be by June?'
'How many of your 50 receipts had errors last week?'
'What could you try to reduce the errors?'
'What will you do first and by when?'
questions.why: Reality establishes where she is now, using facts. The other questions belong to Goal, Options and Way forward.

questions.q: Shelly-Ann asks, 'What should I do about the errors?' Which reply best builds her ability to improve her own work?
o: 'Check each receipt twice from now on.'
'I will ask someone else to do your receipts.'
'The errors are not important this month.'
'What do you think is causing them?'
questions.why: A question that makes her analyse the cause builds her skill and ownership. Giving an instruction does not build her ability, and dismissing the errors fails her.

questions.q: Winston reported his own error, which cost J$6,000. How should Mr Reid respond?
o: Thank him for reporting and help to fix the cause
Warn him that errors cost money
Say nothing to avoid embarrassing him
Share Winston's mistake at the next meeting as an example
questions.why: Thanking people who report their own mistakes keeps problems visible so that they can be fixed. Blame or public embarrassment teaches people to hide errors.

questions.q: The queue ticket idea came from one clerk, but the whole team tested it. What is the fairest recognition?
o: Thank only the clerk who proposed the idea
Thank the supervisor for approving the trial
Credit the clerk and thank the team for testing
Mention it only in the annual staff report
questions.why: Specific, shared credit is fair and encourages both ideas and teamwork. Giving credit to one person ignores the effort of the others.

questions.q: What was the mean (average) weekly number of errors before the checklist?
questions.why: (16 + 14 + 18 + 12) ÷ 4 = 60 ÷ 4 = 15. The sum is 60; dividing by the number of weeks gives the mean.

questions.q: What was the percentage reduction in the mean weekly errors after the checklist?
Errors have crept back up to 11 a week. What should the team leader do first?
o: Abandon the checklist, since it failed
Blame the newest team member
Order a larger kaizen event
Check whether the checklist is still being used
questions.why: The first question is whether the new method is still being followed. If it is not, the remedy is training and checking. If it is, the team investigates other causes.

questions.q: The leader wants to show her manager that the checklist worked. Which evidence is strongest?
o: The single best week after the change, which had 3 errors
A run chart of weekly errors, with the change date and averages
The counter staff's view that things feel better now
The low cost of printing the checklist for each member
questions.why: A run of weekly figures before and after the change, with averages, shows the pattern and the normal ups and downs. One good week or an opinion is not proof, and the printing cost says nothing about results.
